title: Alcohol and your fitness goals
chunks: Alcohol provides about 7 kcal per gram — almost as much as fat — and those calories come with no protein, fiber, or useful nutrients. The calories add up quickly: a beer is roughly 150 kcal, a glass of wine about 120–150 kcal, and a cocktail can be 200–400 kcal or more once mixers are included.

While your body processes alcohol, it deprioritizes burning fat and storing other fuels, because metabolizing alcohol takes precedence. A single night of drinking will not undo your progress, but frequent drinking makes a deficit much harder to maintain and can slow fat loss.

Alcohol can blunt muscle protein synthesis and impair recovery and sleep quality, especially in larger amounts close to training. Heavy drinking the night after a hard session works against the adaptations you trained for.

Drinking also lowers inhibitions around food, which is often where the real calorie damage happens — late-night, high-calorie eating while drinking can easily double the total calories of a night out.

If you choose to drink and want to protect your goals: budget the calories into your day in advance, favor lower-calorie options (spirits with zero-calorie mixers, light beer, dry wine), alternate with water, eat a protein-rich meal beforehand, and keep the quantity modest.

Alcohol is compatible with a flexible approach to nutrition as long as it fits your weekly calories and you keep protein and training on track. The key is planning for it rather than letting it derail the day.
This is general nutrition information, not medical or addiction guidance. If alcohol feels difficult to control, please reach out to a doctor or a qualified professional.
